title: India Just Scrapped All Cotton Import Duties Until October. The Textile Industry Says It Is Not Enough.
excerpt: A 50-70 lakh bale shortfall in domestic cotton supply forced the government's hand. Industry leaders say the relief is welcome but spinning mills need to pass savings down the value chain.
body:
The Indian government on Saturday announced a complete exemption of customs duties on cotton imports for five months, effective June 1 through October 31, 2026. The decision, issued through a Finance Ministry notification, removes both the basic customs duty and the Agriculture Infrastructure and Development Cess on raw cotton — an effective combined rate of about 10.5 percent.

The move is the government's second such intervention in less than a year. A similar exemption ran from August to December 2025. This time, the trigger is a widening gap between domestic cotton production and the textile sector's demand.

## The Numbers Behind the Decision

India's cotton production for the 2025-26 season is estimated at roughly 290-292 lakh bales. The textile and apparel sector's demand, however, is expected to hit 330-340 lakh bales — a shortfall of 50-70 lakh bales that manufacturers cannot bridge without imports.

Cotton prices tell the story plainly. Over the past two months, domestic cotton prices surged from about ₹54,500 per candy (355 kg) to nearly ₹71,000 per candy before softening slightly. The 11 percent import duty on top of already elevated global prices made imported cotton prohibitively expensive for smaller manufacturers.

Raw cotton imports already surged 54.6 percent year-on-year to $1.86 billion in FY26, according to DGFT data. India imports primarily long-staple varieties from the United States, Egypt, Australia, and Brazil — varieties its domestic crop does not produce in sufficient quantities.

## Industry Response: Welcome but Incomplete

The Coimbatore-based Southern India Mills' Association (SIMA) said it had been pushing for the removal of cotton import duties and described the decision as timely. But SIMA and other industry bodies want more: they want spinning mills to pass the savings from cheaper imported cotton down the value chain to yarn buyers, fabric manufacturers, and garment exporters.

Dr. A. Sakthivel, chairman of the Apparel Export Promotion Council (AEPC), made the point explicitly. He urged spinning mills to "rationalise yarn prices" so that garment exporters could secure export orders more competitively. Without that pass-through, he argued, the duty waiver benefits accumulate at the top of the supply chain and never reach the small and medium enterprises that actually produce India's textile exports.

The Confederation of Indian Textile Industry (CITI) framed the stakes in global terms. India's textile and apparel exports fell to $35.79 billion in FY26, a 2.2 percent decline in dollar terms. Readymade garment exports specifically dropped from $16.01 billion to $15.81 billion. With the United States poised to increase its existing 25 percent tariff on Indian goods, every rupee of cost reduction matters.

## The Farmer Question

Cotton farmers, predictably, view duty-free imports differently. Cheap imported cotton depresses domestic prices, reducing their earnings. The Finance Ministry's notification acknowledged this tension, stating the exemption was designed "keeping the interests of domestic farmers in mind." But no specific farmer compensation or price support mechanism was announced alongside the waiver.

## What It Means for NRIs

For Indian Americans and other diaspora members with business ties to India's textile sector — a significant number in the United States, United Kingdom, and the Gulf — the duty waiver signals a government willing to prioritise export competitiveness over protectionism, at least temporarily. India's textile industry employs over 45 million workers and accounts for 8-10 percent of total merchandise exports. Its health matters to the Indian economy in ways that ripple outward.

The waiver expires October 31. What happens then depends on the monsoon, the global cotton harvest, and whether the government decides to make duty-free cotton a permanent feature of its trade architecture.

*Sources: Finance Ministry notification, Mint, The Hindu BusinessLine, Devdiscourse*
author: Diaspora Desk
